Graphics are still messed up on consoles (even PS4 and Xbox One) because not everyone is on the same page when it comes to the legacy luminance issue.

When TV first came out, the technology was iffy and so the amount of luminance in an image was given a fudge factor. Instead of 0-255 to represent how much light was in a particular pixel, 16-235 was used. This allowed for subpar equipment to still show a decent image, at the expense of luminance range. So all TV and movies that are created, even today, adhere to the 16-235 standard.

Computers, however, had high standards for their equipment and decided that 0-255 was the correct range for luminance. So most things created to run on a computer (games included) are expecting to output to that range.

HDTV added the possiblity for HD broadcast and blu-ray content to use 0-255, but it doesn't.

TVs will, depending on how well they work, figure out which space is being used and either expand it or compress the signal as necessary. But it's really tricky to figure out whether a given TV will handle this properly or even consistently (that is, sometimes, half-way through content, the luminance space will switch when the software messes up its analysis).

Consoles exist in their own weird world where they may be generating content in the 0-255 range, compressing it to 16-235, then outputing a signal that is in the 0-255 range. No matter what the TV does, the image will not be right - in this case, everything looks washed out. Or, it may go the exact opposite way, 16-235 content, expanded into the 0-255 range, but then broadcast out as a 16-235 signal. In this case, everything looks really really dark. Almost every console game I've ever seen in the last generation has been messed up in one of these ways. Really annoying especially when you spend a lot of money on a nice TV/monitor.

One example where you could see the issue was Left 4 Dead 2. There was actually a setting buried in the menu to take into account whether you were playing on a TV or a monitor, but it didn't always solve the problem. Play a map from the L4D2 selection then play a map from the L4D1 selection (they added the L4D1 campaigns in a DLC). You will notice that black/white levels are completely different. For me, if the TV is adjusted correctly for the L4D2 map, then the L4D1 map will be way too dark.

At least on a PC, you can tell the computer which type of signal to output, depending on the display device.
